# A revocation right whose evidence belongs to the delegate

**Candidate C013 · Development draft · 22 October 2026**

**Originality verdict:** The broad independence thesis is already substantially occupied. The argument below is a narrower proposal about the allocation of verification costs. It is not a certified new result.

## The problem

Imagine that a cooperative delegates procurement to an exceptionally capable manager. Members can dismiss her immediately. They also receive accurate weekly reports. Nevertheless, every report is assembled from categories she defines, and only she can authorize an investigation into what the categories exclude. Nothing currently indicates misconduct. Is the cooperative's authority over its manager secure?

An easy answer says that dismissal remains legally available. A more demanding answer asks whether members have a usable way of discovering that dismissal is warranted. But this second answer is not our discovery. Cohen and Suzor's *Contesting the public interest in AI governance* (2024), especially §3.3, already connects meaningful contestation with independent information and examines information monopolies and external scrutiny. Relabeling that requirement as “epistemic revocability” would not establish originality.

The remaining question is distributive. Suppose independent investigation exists, but exercising it requires every member to become a procurement expert. Who must bear the cost of maintaining a practical capacity to reconsider delegation?

## A narrower proposal

When an institution represents a delegation as subject to continuing control, and the delegation foreseeably concentrates access to information needed to exercise that control, the arrangement should normally finance an adequate means of independent checking. Providing an abstract permission to purchase an audit does not discharge this responsibility when the audit's cost predictably defeats the promised control.

This is a claim about the responsibilities created by an institutional arrangement. It is not a claim that every delegate must personally pay for unlimited scrutiny. A small voluntary club might share the costs explicitly. A powerful organization governing dependent members might have to absorb them. The relevant question is whether the people asked to authorize the arrangement are offered practically usable control on terms they can fairly be expected to meet.

Compare two versions of the cooperative. In the first, the common budget pays for a periodically selected independent auditor, and members can trigger a limited supplementary inquiry at a manageable threshold. In the second, each dissenter must privately purchase an equally good audit. Assume the same manager, evidence, performance, and formal dismissal procedure. An affluent member could investigate in either version. Ordinary members cannot investigate in the second.

The difference is not a difference in the manager's trustworthiness. Nor does it establish that she lacks legitimate authority in every transaction. It concerns the distribution of the capacity that supposedly makes her continuing authority answerable to members. The second arrangement turns collective control into an option exercised mainly by the wealthy.

## Why the duty follows

The proposed argument has three steps. First, a right offered as a safeguard cannot do its justificatory work if its foreseeable exercise conditions exclude its intended holders. Second, delegation can itself generate these conditions by concentrating expertise, records, and practical familiarity in the delegate. Third, the institution that deliberately creates that dependence has a stronger responsibility to arrange proportionate checking than an unrelated outsider has to subsidize any investigation whatsoever.

The controversial step is the third. It might be defended as a principle against imposing the costs of an institutional safeguard on those whose dependence makes the safeguard necessary. The argument therefore does not infer a positive duty merely from the desirability of an audit. It connects the duty to an organization's own claim that its concentration of authority remains controllable.

This also explains why independence is a matter of powers rather than labels. An auditor paid from the common budget can be independent if the manager cannot suppress findings or dismiss the auditor at will. Conversely, an outside contractor can be captured if the manager determines every question the contractor may ask. Separate employment is neither necessary nor sufficient for the proposed protection.

## Limits and objections

The strongest objection is that fiduciary duties, republican freedom, and fair access to institutional remedies already entail all of this. That objection is serious. The unavailable DeMott and Pettit texts listed in the access register are necessary comparisons. Until they are read, this draft should be treated as a possible synthesis or application, not a new principle.

A second objection is that checking defeats the point of delegation. Members delegate because independent verification is expensive. The answer cannot be that every decision requires duplication. Adequacy should depend on stakes, reversibility, existing public information, and the reliability of alternative checks. Sampling, pooled expertise, and protected whistleblowing might be enough. Some low-stakes arrangements need no standing audit at all.

A third objection concerns confidentiality. Independent checking need not mean public release of every record. A trusted intermediary can verify a disputed question without exposing irrelevant personal information. The required power is to investigate and communicate a warranted challenge through an effective route.

## What would make this worth an essay?

Its philosophical significance would lie in showing that maintaining revocable authority creates a distinctive responsibility to distribute the costs of knowing when to revoke. But the case is not yet made that this responsibility differs from familiar fairness and fiduciary principles. The appropriate next test is a case in which those principles appear satisfied while verification costs still undermine the claimed authority. If no such case survives, retain this as a useful institutional application and remove it from the originality shortlist.

- Cohen, Tegan, and Nicolas P. Suzor. 2024. “Contesting the public interest in AI governance.” *Internet Policy Review* 13(3). https://doi.org/10.14763/2024.3.1794. Full text available; relevant information-independence discussion read.
- DeMott, Deborah A. 2014. “The Fiduciary Character of Agency and the Interpretation of Instructions.” https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/faculty_scholarship/3129/. Repository description only; full text requested.
- Pettit, Philip. 2000. “Democracy, Electoral and Contestatory.” *Designing Democratic Institutions*, pp. 105–144. https://ppettit.scholar.princeton.edu/publications/democracy-electoral-and-contestatory. Publication verified; linked full text inaccessible.
